result.killer: No single killer was found. The weak points are partial: the state FWCMS portal is mandatory and is where all filing happens, the deadlines are fixed and the same for every employer (so trackers add little), law-firm reminders are free, and EOR/agent services exist (Playroll, Mercans).
result.reason: I found nothing that kills the idea outright. No Cambodian HR product with a work-permit or FMQ module turned up; MIHCM claims Cambodia compliance, but I could not confirm any permit feature. Whether FWCMS sends its own reminders is still unverified. Still, the case for software is weak. Every deadline is the same for all employers: quota applications run 1 Sep-30 Nov, renewals are due by 31 Mar and permits expire 31 Dec. So tracking each worker's expiry date adds little, and law firms' free newsletters (KPMG, DFDL, Andersen) already send the reminders. All filing must happen inside the state FWCMS portal, which runs on LACMS data, and I found no sign of an outside API. Employer-of-record firms (Playroll, Mercans) and agents handle permits as a service. I found no current count of employers or permits; the newest figure was 118,280 permit registrations in Jan-Aug 2018. Agent prices were not found.

coverage.category: 8. Beekeepers
coverage.found: No regulated register or MAFF registration scheme found for beekeepers or honey producers (English and Khmer searches). A 2025 review in Insects (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC11766281/) names lack of official documentation and data, weak organisation of beekeepers, and unregulated bee imports as gaps, so there is no mandatory recurring duty to build on. Only voluntary activity exists: the CBHE federation of about 780 wild-honey collectors in six provinces runs a participatory guarantee system (PGS) for the 'Khmum Prey' label (NTFP-EP, https://ntfp.org/?p=3479). Nothing found on hive registration, apiary movement records or honey export traceability. Not a regulated-register category in Cambodia; only a weak, community-led certification niche.

coverage.category: 10. Well drillers and water abstraction
coverage.found: The 2007 Law on Water Resources Management lists use of groundwater and aquifers for commercial purposes among activities needing a MOWRAM water-use licence (https://leap.unep.org/en/countries/kh/national-legislation/law-water-resources-management-kingdom-cambodia). No prakas, sub-decree or register specific to well drillers or drilling permits found in Khmer or English. A June 2025 national dialogue (SEI, https://www.sei.org/about-sei/press-room/cambodia-groundwater-regulation/; the page itself returned 403 on fetch, so this rests on search snippets) says groundwater governance is fragmented with limited regulatory framework and enforcement, and that MOWRAM is only starting a national groundwater framework. Private rural drillers operate on a merchant basis (World Bank Mirep note, 2010, dated) with no association or registry found. Possible future trigger if the groundwater framework produces driller licensing or abstraction reporting; nothing in force found. Unverified: whether commercial groundwater licences are actually issued and how many holders exist; the full law text and any MOWRAM licence forms were not opened.

Cremation is mostly done at pagodas; Phnom Penh City Hall closed the last traditional temple crematoriums in 2010 (https://english.cambodiadaily.com/2010/02/19/capitals-last-traditional-crematoriums-ordered-to-close/) and later offered free cremation for the poor after a public row over temple price lists (https://www.asianews.it/en/south-east-asia/cambodia/phnom-penh-free-funeral-rites-for-the-poor, undated). Only about three funeral homes existed in Phnom Penh in 2017, so the market is tiny and informal. No recurring filing duty identified. Unchecked: current Ministry of Health cremation or burial permit procedure, Ministry of Cults and Religion rules for pagoda crematoria, any recent City Hall funeral-fee prakas.

result.competitor: No software or app was found for the owner-side workflow, in English or Khmer. No public list of licensed inspectors was found. The likely real competition is a service: lift OEM agents and maintenance contractors (Hitachi, KONE via Comin, and others) who already hold maintenance contracts and can bundle certificate filing and the 2-yearly inspections. Law firms and permit agents can also file at the One-Window office. Competition check was limited to web search.
result.duty: Prakas No. 008 DNS/K.K.C/PRK (MLMUPC, 29 Jan 2026), in force on issue according to law-firm summaries. Each lift needs a certificate of elevator use from MLMUPC via the One-Window Service Office (review up to 21 working days, certificate valid indefinitely, one certificate per lift, displayed on site). A quality and safety inspection by an MLMUPC-licensed inspector is due every 2 years, and the inspector issues a certification letter of elevator safety and quality once any defects are fixed. Lifts operating before the Prakas have a 1-year transition (about late Jan 2027). Penalties: written warning, suspension or revocation of the certificate, and an immediate stop order for operating without one. Prakas 033 (31 Mar 2026) adds Level 1 and Level 2 licences for installers, valid 3 years. Fees not found. Official Prakas text not found; only law-firm summaries (Rajah & Tann, Andersen).
result.market: There is no official register of lifts. Wikipedia reports about 1,902 high-rise buildings in Phnom Penh (about 1,877 of 14-20 floors as of June 2025; community-edited and approximate). A 2022 study counted 2,534 high-rises built nationally since 2000, 1,674 of them in Phnom Penh. Add hotels and low-rise buildings with lifts and that is perhaps 2,000-4,000 owners with several thousand lifts (my extrapolation). Most are mid-size or large owners and developers, not micro-businesses.
result.reason: The duty is real. MLMUPC Prakas 008 (29 Jan 2026) requires a certificate of use for each lift, applied for at the One-Window office (21 working days to review) and displayed on site. Licensed inspections are due every 2 years. Pre-existing lifts have 1 year, to about Jan 2027. Penalties: warning, suspension or revocation, or an order to stop operating. No software found. But the certificate is one-off (valid indefinitely) and inspections come every 2 years, so frequency is low. Buyers are mid-to-large building owners, not tiny firms. Market is roughly 1,900 high-rises in Phnom Penh (Wikipedia, approximate). Licensed lift installers and maintainers will probably bundle the paperwork as a service. Better as a one-off done-for-you filing service near the deadline than as SaaS.

result.competitor: The World Bank Water and Sanitation Program built the Enterprise Resource Management System (ERMS), a management and billing application for Cambodian water service providers. GRET's business-development-services package for private operators lists it among its tools; I could not read the GRET PDF to confirm cost or uptake. KOBELCO ran a JETRO-backed pilot with Kampong Thom Water Supply covering everything from the treatment plant to bill collection. GEOCRAFT has an AQUA Crew mapping project with MISTI. Banks such as KB PRASAC and ABA already collect bills for private suppliers. I found no commercial Cambodian vendor selling billing or compliance software to private operators, and no product that files reports into the monitoring system; whether that system needs manual entry is not reached. JETRO notes that meter reading and bill collection are still mostly manual.
result.duty: The Law on Clean Water Supply Management (NS/RKM/0323/002, 11 Mar 2023) is in force, according to FAOLEX/LEAP and DFDL. It requires a feasibility-study permit, a business licence and an operating certificate from MISTI. Expansion needs prior MISTI approval and at least 80% supply of the approved area. Penalties run from warnings and licence suspension or revocation up to fines and prison. The claim's "tariff review every 5 years" is done by MISTI, not by the operator, so it is not an operator workflow. Licences reportedly last 20 years, so licensing is rare rather than recurring. I found no source giving the frequency or content of periodic operator reporting. The World Bank says only that operator KPIs are "increasingly available" in MISTI's Water Supply Monitoring System; who enters the data and how often is not reached. The recurring compliance duty is therefore unconfirmed.
result.market: A MISTI statement (March 2025), as quoted in search results, gives 454 private water operators serving 55% of 1.4 million connections; I could not open the MISTI page myself because it was blocked. There were 258 licences in 2019 (World Bank). The ERMS description says many suppliers are unlicensed. The market is small: about 450 buyers, many of them family firms.
result.reason: The licensing duty is real and current, but its core steps are rare: 20-year licences, a MISTI-led tariff review every 5 years, and occasional expansion approvals. I could not confirm a recurring operator reporting duty or its frequency. There is a donor-built billing and management tool (World Bank ERMS), and banks already handle bill collection. The real day-to-day pain is manual meter reading and billing, which is a generic utility-billing tool rather than compliance software. With about 454 operators and limited ability to pay, the market is small. A billing-plus-monitoring-system-reporting tool could still work if MISTI requires periodic KPI submission, but that is not verified.

result.competitor: The free state FPCS-GDI app (iOS, Android and web, from the General Department of Immigration, released Oct 2019) already does the core foreigner-reporting job. Its store listing says it captures guest information at check-in, scans ID documents to extract the data, uploads documents, tracks past submissions and has a daily statistics dashboard. So the manual per-occupant data entry is already eased by the state's own OCR. I found no third-party FPCS integration, API or bulk upload in English or Khmer searches. International PMS products are present in Cambodia (mycloud via its partner Techsider, 2019; Softinn), but I found no evidence that any of them file to FPCS. What remains open is the Sub-Decree 03 resident register and the 1-year entry/exit log, though paper satisfies both.
result.duty: Real and in force. Sub-Decree 03 was issued on 5 Jan 2026 and covers "concentrated residential areas", which explicitly include hotels, guesthouses, dormitories, resorts, apartments, pagodas and churches. Owners and managers must: keep accurate resident records (on paper or electronically); report changes of residency to the police and the commune or sangkat office; report foreigners within 24 hours; check that a foreigner can lawfully reside in Cambodia before letting them stay; keep CCTV footage for at least 90 days; and keep entry and exit records for at least 1 year. The Rajah & Tann summary (fetched) does not give fines or an effective date. Andersen and blogs cite KHR 400,000 and USD 1,000 per undocumented occupant, but I could not check this against the official Khmer text. The separate FPCS duty (operators report each foreign guest within 24 hours in the GDI app) dates from 2020 and is tied to visa extensions. One older source cites a fine of KHR 30,000 per foreigner. The duty recurs with every check-in.
result.market: CEIC, republishing Ministry of Tourism data, lists about 2,272 guesthouses in Cambodia in 2024 (Phnom Penh 321, Siem Reap 293). I did not find the number of hotel establishments. CEIC gives 47,655 hotel rooms in 2023 and 32,134 guesthouse rooms in 2022. Adding hotels, homestays, dormitories and rental apartments, the total is probably about 4,000 to 10,000 properties (my estimate, not a register count). Boreys, condos and factory dormitories also carry the Sub-Decree duty.
result.reason: The duty is real, recurring and enforced through visa linkage and police spot checks. But the core foreigner report is already handled by the free GDI FPCS app, which includes passport scanning and submission history. What is left (the resident register, the 1-year entry/exit log, 24h reminders) can legally be kept on paper. Buyers are mostly owner-run guesthouses that are price-sensitive and probably have little willingness to pay. There is no known FPCS API, so an add-on can't automate filing and would mean entering data twice. A bigger PMS bundle would compete with established vendors. The market is small, perhaps a few thousand properties. A niche add-on for boreys and dormitories may be worth more than one for guesthouses.

result.competitor: The mandatory state portal FWCMS (run with E-Solution (Cambodia) Co. Ltd since 2016) already handles quota, permit and employment-card filing online. Once LACMS is linked, it can auto-generate lists of Cambodian and foreign staff (per secondary summary). Whether FWCMS sends expiry alerts is unverified. Law firms and advisers (KPMG, DFDL, Andersen, Tilleke, VDB Loi, HBS Law, Sciaroni) and employer-of-record firms such as Playroll offer filing as a service. I found no Cambodia HR software with a work-permit or FMQ module, and no standalone tracker (English and Khmer searches). Current agent prices were not found.
result.duty: Confirmed in force. MLVT Notification 025/26 (31 Aug 2026) covers all factories and enterprises that employ or plan to employ foreigners in 2027. They must apply for the 2027 FMQ on FWCMS (fwcms.mlvt.gov.kh) between 1 Sep and 30 Nov 2026. An approved FMQ is a prerequisite for work permits. Foreigners must get a permit within 90 days of first entry. LACMS must be linked with FWCMS. Missing the FMQ draws a Labour Inspector fine of KHR 12.2m-18m (~USD 3,050-4,500; Art. 369 Labour Law, Prakas 326). Working without a permit draws KHR 50.4m (Joint Prakas 498), as reported in a 2025 summary. The quota cap is 10% of the Cambodian workforce (3% office, 6% skilled, 1% unskilled); exceeding it requires an application under Prakas 277/20. The cycle is annual, with permits running per calendar year. Sources are law-firm and Big-4 summaries; I did not open the official MLVT text.
result.market: Not found. My searches turned up no published MLVT count of foreign work permits or of enterprises holding an FMQ for 2024-2025. Who carries the duty is broad: companies, branches, representative offices, NGOs and associations with any foreign staff. The number of small employers with foreigners remains unverified.
result.reason: The duty is real and in force. KPMG and DFDL summaries of MLVT Notification 025/26 say every enterprise employing foreigners in 2027 must get FMQ approval on FWCMS between 1 Sep and 30 Nov 2026. Work permits need that quota, new arrivals have 90 days, and LACMS must be linked to FWCMS. Fines run from KHR 12.2m to 18m (Labour Law Art. 369). I found no third-party tracker software. Still, the required state portal FWCMS already does the filing, and law firms and agents sell the done-for-you service. That leaves software only reminders and quota-ratio checks. The cycle is once a year plus new hires. The buyers are scattered foreign-run firms that already pay agents. I found no market count. Best sold as an add-on to the K01 payroll/LACMS pack.

result.competitor: MoC registrationservices.gov.kh (free state portal); DFDL and Emerhub filing services; Deloitte and KPMG advisories
result.duty: ADCE annual filing within 3 months before the registration anniversary plus 15 days grace. Fine of KHR 2,000,000 per year missed. Three consecutive years unfiled can mark the company inactive. Penalty relief under Announcement 0051 (Jan 2026), extended by MoC Notification 2463 (10 Jul 2026).
result.market: not_reached: no register count found. The duty covers limited companies, foreign branches and representative offices, not sole proprietors.
result.reason: The duty is real, but it is narrower than the claim. The annual declaration (ADCE) applies to limited companies, foreign branches and representative offices, not sole proprietors. The window runs from three months before the registration anniversary, plus a 15-day grace period. The penalty is KHR 2,000,000 per missed year. Prakas 044 (26 May 2026) only lists the ADCE as a topic, and I found no text showing it changes the rules. The state portal registrationservices.gov.kh handles filing, now behind CamDigiKey, and the MoC sends reminders. Law firms and company-secretary providers (DFDL, Emerhub) sell it as a service. I found no dedicated ADCE software. Buyers are corporate service providers, and filing is a single online form, so willingness to pay is low. It is best treated as an add-on to K03. I did not find a count of affected entities.

Duty is real: DFDL says MoE Prakas 9540 (26 Nov 2025) requires an Environmental Protection Agreement and management plan from existing and new factories with USD 50k-500k capital, 30 working day review, with fines, suspension and revocation. Not confirmed: the six sectors, the filing deadline, the periodic reporting frequency, and the market size. I ran no competitor search. The duty looks mostly like a one-off document for consultants, with no clear recurring workflow. Buyers are fragmented and the legal text is probably Khmer-only. Together these make it a weak software fit, so I scored it 3.

Prakas 228 (28 Oct 2009, MoC) is listed as in force and requires jewellery traders to obtain MoC permission. I could not confirm the claimed 12-month NBC licence, the Type A/B split, renewal frequency, penalties or any register/reporting duty. I found no full text and no 2025-26 gold-specific rule. The 2007 AML/CFT law covers precious-metal dealers, but I found no CAFIU guidance for jewellers. I found no competing software, and no shop count. A licence renewal is infrequent (about once a year), the market is small and informal, and there is no recurring filing workflow for software to ease. The score is low.

Sub-Decree 190 (2011) is real and was the current framework in every source found. I found no 2025-26 replacement, but that is not confirmed either way. The buyer pool is tiny: a Cambodia Daily list named about 77 licensed agencies (undated). The licence is renewed only every 5 years, so frequency is low and the pain is mostly one-off. Agencies are few and each filing is occasional, so willingness to pay is weak. I found no agency-specific software and no state portal for outbound agencies. Only the inbound-worker FWCMS portal turned up, which is a different job. Per-worker file reporting duties were not confirmed. I did not retrieve the primary texts of Prakas 463 or the penalties. I suggest 2, below the provisional 3.

Prakas 384 (2 Oct 2020) exists, as does Prakas 414 (2019) on permits for trading, stockpiling and distribution. Only summaries were readable. The PDF was unreadable and I could not confirm the record-keeping, renewal frequency or penalty rules. No current shop count exists: the only figures are a 2013 two-province survey (about 100 shops) and unknown private-vet numbers. I found no competing software or state app, but the search was thin and untargeted. The market is small and informal, buyers pay little, and enforcement looks weak. The workflow is mostly a permit and licensing process, not a recurring filing. That makes it a poor fit for a solo founder, so I score it low.

Duty is partly confirmed. The MME rules page lists two prakas: 13 Sep 2024 (operation of petroleum, LPG and joint stations) and 29 Apr 2025 (delegating LPG cylinder storage station permits to town/district administrations). I did not find the 23 Jul 2024 safety certificate prakas on that page. I could not read the texts, so renewal cycle, reporting duty, fees and penalties are unknown. I ran no competitor search for software. Market: the Ministry of Commerce counted more than 6,300 stations nationwide in March 2026 (per a search summary), but I found no LPG shop count. Scoring is low because permits are infrequent and are handled by local administrations, buyers are fragmented, and the software job is unclear.
